entry: Telescope that gathers and focuses mainly visible light from the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]]. Optical telescopes produce a magnified image for direct viewing, photography, or data collection through electronic image sensors. The three primary types are refracting telescopes, which use [[Lens|lenses]] and less commonly [[Prism (optics)|prisms]]; reflecting telescopes, which use [[Mirror|mirrors]]; and catadioptric telescopes, which combine both. Resolving power depends on the diameter of the objective, the primary lens or mirror, while light-gathering power depends on its area. The first documents describing a refracting telescope date from 1608, when spectacle maker Hans Lippershey filed a patent in the Netherlands. [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] made improved designs within a year and was the first to publish astronomical results with one. Reflecting telescopes, developed in the 17th century, avoid chromatic aberration. Uses include [[Astronomy|observational astronomy]], ornithology, pilotage, reconnaissance, and watching sports and performances.

Healthcare practice concerned with examining the eyes for visual defects. Optometrists prescribe corrective lenses, such as [[Glasses|glasses]] and contact lenses, detect eye abnormalities, and monitor and treat ocular diseases such as [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]]. The term comes from [[Ancient Greek]] ὄψις (ópsis), meaning eye, and μέτρον (métron), meaning measure. In the United States and Canada, optometrists hold a four-year Doctor of Optometry degree taken after a bachelor's degree. In the United Kingdom, optometrists may also prescribe medications and perform various surgeries, and the Doctor of Optometry degree is rarer. Training varies greatly between countries, from certificate courses to doctoral degrees. Some optometrists also conduct academic research on eye conditions.

Genus of flowering plants in the [[Cactus|cactus]] family, commonly called prickly pear. Many species have flavorful fruit, and the fruit and stems are edible. The Barbary fig (*Opuntia ficus-indica*) is the most common culinary species. The prickly pear was domesticated in central [[Mexico]] between 8,000 and 9,000 years ago. Native to the [[Americas]], the plant has been introduced to Australia, southern Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Africa. Where introduced, some species become aggressive [[Invasive species|invasive species]]. Cacti are vulnerable to alterations in precipitation and temperature driven by climate change.

American multinational technology company selling [[Database|database]] software, enterprise applications, and cloud infrastructure. Co-founded on June 16, 1977, in Santa Clara, California, by Bob Miner, Ed Oates, and [[Larry Ellison]] as Software Development Laboratories. The name drew on the codename of a 1977 project for the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], Oracle's first customer. The company was renamed Relational Software in 1979 and Oracle Systems Corporation in 1983. Its initial public offering took place on March 12, 1986. Its core application software covers enterprise resource planning, human capital management, customer experience, and supply chain management.

Practice of keeping the mouth clean and free of disease and bad breath. Regular brushing of the teeth and cleaning between them prevent dental disease. General guidelines for adults advise brushing at least twice a day with fluoridated toothpaste. A toothbrush removes only about 50% of plaque from tooth surfaces, so interdental cleaning with floss, tape, or interdental brushes is considered equally important. The most common dental diseases are [[Tooth decay|tooth decay]] (cavities) and gum diseases, including gingivitis and periodontitis. Caries affect 60–90% of schoolchildren in industrialized countries, and severe gum disease causes at least one-third of adult tooth loss. Since before recorded history, people have cleaned their teeth with chew sticks, twigs, bird feathers, animal bones, and porcupine quills. In the Muslim world, the miswak, a twig or root, has been used since the [[Islamic Golden Age]].

Sexual activity involving stimulation of the genitals with the mouth, lips, or tongue. [[Cunnilingus]] is oral stimulation of the vulva, [[Fellatio]] of the penis, and [[Anilingus]] of the anus. Oral sex may be foreplay or an erotic act in its own right, and it may be practiced by people of any sexual orientation. Like other sexual activity, it can transmit [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], but the risk, especially for HIV, is significantly lower than for vaginal or anal sex. Most countries do not ban the practice, although it is often regarded as taboo. Oral sex alone does not result in pregnancy, but a potential risk exists if semen contacts the vaginal area. Some people practice it to preserve *technical virginity*. It is not necessarily an effective method of preventing sexually transmitted infections, although it has been recommended as safe sex.

Coastal city in northwest [[Algeria]], the second-largest city in the country after [[Algiers]]. It lies 432 km (268 mi) west-southwest of the capital and is the capital of Oran Province. The city had a population of 803,329 in 2008, and its metropolitan area has about 1,500,000 residents. The name is thought to derive from a Berber expression meaning place of lions. Founded in the 10th century, it was occupied by the Spanish in 1509 and reconquered in 1792 by the bey Mohamed el-Kebir. The French took the city in 1831 and developed it rapidly. The Vichy government held Oran during [[World War II]] until Allied forces captured it in late 1942. After independence in 1962, it remained the economic capital of western Algeria.

Major river in southern Africa, the longest river in [[South Africa]]. It rises in the [[Drakensberg]] mountains on the border with [[Lesotho]], where it is called the Senqu, and flows westward through South Africa to the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. With a total length of 2,432 km (1,511 mi), its basin extends into Lesotho, South Africa, and [[Namibia]]. The river forms international borders between South Africa and Lesotho and between South Africa and Namibia. It was named in honor of the Dutch House of Orange by the Dutch explorer Robert Jacob Gordon. The Augrabies Falls are where the river descends 56 m (184 ft) in a course of 18 km (11 mi). The river supports irrigation and hydroelectric power in the South African economy.

Color between yellow and red on the spectrum of visible light. The human eye perceives orange under light with a dominant wavelength between roughly 585 and 620 nanometers. In traditional color theory it is a secondary color of pigments, produced by mixing yellow and red, and in the RGB model it is a tertiary color. The color is named after the fruit. Before the late 15th century, Europeans had no separate word for it and called it yellow-red. Many fruits and vegetables, such as carrots, pumpkins, and sweet potatoes, owe their orange color to carotenes. Surveys in Europe and the United States find orange most associated with amusement, warmth, energy, danger, and autumn. It is the national color of the [[Netherlands]] and the House of Orange, and the political color of [[Christian democracy|Christian democratic]] parties.

Citrus fruit of the sweet orange tree, *Citrus × sinensis*. It is a hybrid between the [[Pomelo|pomelo]] and the [[Mandarin orange|mandarin orange]], though its chloroplast genome, and therefore its maternal line, is that of the pomelo. The fruit originated in a region encompassing southern [[China]], northeast India, and Myanmar, and the earliest mention of the sweet orange is in Chinese literature in 314 BC. Orange trees are widely grown in tropical and subtropical areas, and the fruit is eaten fresh or processed for juice or fragrant peel. In 2024, 67 million tonnes of oranges were grown worldwide, with [[Brazil]] producing 23% of the total, followed by China and Mexico. Oranges first appear in Western art in the [[Arnolfini Portrait]] by Jan van Eyck. The tree is a small evergreen, averaging 9 to 10 m (30 to 33 ft) in height.

Great ape of the genus *Pongo*, native to the rainforests of [[Borneo]] and [[Sumatra]]. Orangutans were once considered a single species, but in 1996 they were divided into the Bornean orangutan and the Sumatran orangutan. A third species, the Tapanuli orangutan, was identified in 2017. The most arboreal of the great apes, they have long arms, reddish-brown hair, and spend most of their time in trees. Dominant adult males develop cheek pads and make long calls that attract females and intimidate rivals. They are the most solitary of the great apes, and fruit is the most important part of their diet. Orangutans are among the most intelligent [[Primate|primates]], using tools and building sleeping nests each night. All three species are critically endangered. Threats include habitat destruction and [[Deforestation|deforestation]] for palm oil cultivation and logging, poaching, and the illegal pet trade.

[[Spider|Spider]] family whose members build spiral wheel-shaped webs. The family Araneidae is among the largest spider families, alongside Salticidae and Linyphiidae. Members have eight similar eyes, hairy or spiny legs, and no stridulating organs. Builders first construct a framework of nonsticky silk, then add a final spiral covered in sticky droplets. Many spin a new web each day, consuming the old one toward evening. Their webs are generally free of the debris that collects in webs of other species, such as black widow spiders.

Curved path of an object around a point, under an attracting force. In celestial mechanics, an orbit is the trajectory of an object such as a planet around a [[Star|star]], a natural satellite around a planet, or an artificial satellite around a planet, moon, asteroid, or [[Lagrange point]]. Normally the term refers to a regularly repeating trajectory. To a close approximation, planets and satellites follow elliptic orbits, with the center of mass at a focal point of the ellipse, as described by [[Johannes Kepler|Kepler]]'s laws of planetary motion. [[Isaac Newton]] showed that Kepler's laws follow from his theory of gravitation, under which orbits are conic sections. Newtonian mechanics explains gravity as an inverse-square force and suffices for most situations. [[Albert Einstein]]'s general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as curvature of spacetime, is more accurate, with orbits following geodesics.

Circuit of the Moon around Earth, stable but highly complex. It orbits Earth prograde, taking about 27.3 days per revolution against the fixed stars and 29.5 days relative to the Sun. Its average distance from Earth's center is 384,400 km (238,900 mi), about 60 Earth radii. Earth and the Moon orbit a shared [[Barycenter|barycenter]] about 4,670 km (2,900 miles) from Earth's center. The orbital plane is inclined about 5.1° from the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]]. Its gravitational interactions with Earth and the Sun make it the oldest three-body problem of astronomy.

Field of classical mechanics concerned with the motion of spacecraft, also called astrodynamics. It applies ballistics and celestial mechanics to rockets, satellites, and other spacecraft, using laws of motion and universal gravitation derived by [[Isaac Newton]]. Mission planners use it to predict the results of propulsive maneuvers, including orbital plane changes and interplanetary transfers. [[General relativity]] is more exact and is sometimes needed for greater accuracy or in high-gravity situations, such as orbits near the Sun. [[Johannes Kepler|Kepler]] first modeled planetary orbits to a high degree of accuracy. In 1801, [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] helped recover the dwarf planet [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] using a method that needed only three observations. Modern orbit determination is essential to operate all types of satellites and space probes. Hohmann transfers, efficient elliptical paths between circular orbits, enable orbit adjustments with minimal fuel.

Toothed whale, the largest member of the oceanic [[Dolphin|dolphin]] family. Also called the killer whale, the orca is recognizable by its mostly black upper body, white underside, and white eye patches. It inhabits a wide range of marine environments, from Arctic to Antarctic regions to tropical seas. [[Apex predator|Apex predators]], orcas eat bony fish, sharks, rays, seals, dolphins, and whales, and populations often specialize in particular prey. Highly social, they form stable matrilineal pods, and hunting techniques and vocal behaviors are passed down through generations. The IUCN lists the orca as data deficient, since multiple types may represent distinct species, while some local populations are endangered. Trained to perform in marine parks, a practice criticized as unethical, captive orcas have injured or killed handlers, but no fatal attack has been recorded in the wild.

Intentional plantation of trees or shrubs maintained for food production. Orchards comprise fruit- or nut-producing trees, generally grown commercially, and are sometimes a feature of large gardens. Most temperate-zone orchards are laid out in a regular grid with grass or bare soil beneath the trees. Common layouts include the square, rectangular, quincunx, triangular, and hexagonal methods. Most modern commercial orchards plant a single variety, although genetic diversity could provide resilience to pests and diseases. In the United States, the most extensive orchards are apple and orange orchards, the latter usually called groves. The largest apple orchard area is in eastern [[Washington (state)|Washington state]], and extensive orange orchards are found in Florida and southern California. In [[Canada]], the Niagara Peninsula is known as the Canada Fruitbelt. In [[Spain]], Murcia is a major citrus orchard area.

Member of the family Orchidaceae, one of the two largest families of flowering plants. The family contains about 28,000 accepted species in around 700 genera, or 6–11% of all seed plant species. Orchids are cosmopolitan, living on every continent except Antarctica, and the richest diversity is in the [[Tropics|tropics]]. Many species are epiphytes that grow on trees. Their flowers are highly specialized for insect pollinators, attracting them by color, pattern, scent, [[Pheromone|pheromones]], or mimicry of female insects. The seeds are very small and depend on fungal partners for germination. Most orchid flowers have three sepals and three petals, and one petal forms a modified lip called the labellum. The genus *Orchis* is named from [[Ancient Greek]] ὄρχις (órkhis), meaning testicle, for the twin tubers of some species.

Nizari Isma'ili Shia military order. Founded by Hasan-i Sabbah in 1090, it held a network of mountain castles in Persia and Syria, including Alamut Castle. Its members carried out [[Assassination|assassinations]] across the [[Levant]] during the [[Crusades]], believed to have killed hundreds over nearly 200 years, including Fatimids, Abbasids, Seljuks, and Crusaders. In 1253 the order began to collapse under the Mongol campaign against the Nizaris, and by 1256 its network had been defeated. The English word assassin derives from *hashshashin*, which is linked to hashish, although the association with hashish is contested.

Set of conventions determining which arithmetic operations to perform first. The rank of an operation is its precedence, and operations with higher precedence are performed first. The conventional order is parentheses, [[Exponentiation|exponentiation]], multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Operations of equal precedence are evaluated from left to right. Thus 1 + 2 × 3 equals 7, not 9. Exponents were introduced in the 16th and 17th centuries and given precedence over addition and multiplication, so 3 + 5² = 28 and 3 × 5² = 75. Parentheses override the convention, as in (2 + 3) × 4 = 20. Some calculators and [[Computer programming|programming languages]] adopt different conventions.

Differential equation dependent on only a single independent variable. Its unknowns are one or more functions, and it involves the derivatives of those functions. The term ordinary contrasts with [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]], which may involve more than one independent variable, and with stochastic differential equations, in which the modeled process is random. They arise in physics, astronomy, meteorology, chemistry, biology, ecology, and economics. [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]'s second law of motion is a simple example. An equation is linear if it can be written as a linear combination of the dependent variable and its derivatives, and autonomous if it does not depend on the independent variable. Many mathematicians, including Newton, [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]], and [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]], have studied them.

Method for estimating the unknown parameters in a [[Linear regression|linear regression]] model. OLS chooses parameters by minimizing the sum of the squared differences between observed values of the dependent variable and the values predicted by the linear function of the independent variables. Geometrically, this is the sum of the squared distances, parallel to the dependent variable's axis, between each data point and the regression surface. Under the Gauss–Markov theorem, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator when errors are homoscedastic and serially uncorrelated. If the errors are also normally distributed with zero mean, OLS is the maximum likelihood estimator. The method is sensitive to outliers and to violations of its assumptions, such as heteroscedasticity, which can lead to inefficient or biased estimates. Legendre published it in 1805, and Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1809.

Second of six periods of the Paleozoic Era, following the [[Cambrian]] and preceding the [[Silurian]]. It was named after the Welsh Ordovices and defined by Charles Lapworth in 1879 to resolve a dispute between Adam Sedgwick and Roderick Murchison. The period ended with the Ordovician–Silurian extinction events. Invertebrates such as molluscs and arthropods dominated the oceans, and the first land plants appeared. Fish, the world's first true vertebrates, continued to evolve. Southern continents were assembled into [[Gondwana]], which reached the [[South Pole]].

Rock or sediment containing valuable minerals, typically metals, that can be mined and processed at a profit. Ore grade refers to the concentration of the desired material, and a rock counts as ore only when its metals are worth the cost of extraction. Unwanted rock mixed with the ore, called gangue, is separated by flotation or magnetic methods, and the leftover waste is called tailings. Minerals of interest are generally oxides, sulfides, silicates, or native metals such as [[Copper|copper]] or [[Gold|gold]]. Ore is treated, often by [[Smelting|smelting]], to extract the metals. Some ores may pose threats to health or surrounding ecosystems. The word ore is of Anglo-Saxon origin, meaning lump of metal.

Emigrant wagon route across North America, about 2,170 miles (3,490 km) long. It connected the [[Missouri River]] to valleys in Oregon Territory and was laid by fur traders and trappers from about 1811 to 1840. The first migrant wagon train was organized in Independence, Missouri, in 1836. Traffic was especially heavy from 1846 to 1869, when about 400,000 settlers, farmers, miners, and ranchers used the trail and its offshoots. Use declined after the first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869. Modern highways, such as Interstate 80 and Interstate 84, follow parts of the route.
